summary:
Georgia's Parliament passed the package "On Family Values and Protection of Minors" on 17 September 2024 by 84 votes to 0, and it was signed into law on 3 October 2024. It prohibits all surgical operations and medical interventions for gender reassignment for people of all ages, and prohibits entering any gender "different from his own" on state or identity documents. The same package bars adoption of a minor by people who do not identify "as their gender", voids public or private labour obligations "aimed at neglecting biological sex", bans radio and television broadcasting, advertising and public gatherings that promote belonging to a gender different from one's own, and bans pride events and public displays of the rainbow flag. It also outlaws "alternative marriage unions" and designates 17 May as a holiday for the sanctity of the family.

A 2024 bill was described as seeking to make being transgender illegal and to remove all transgender recognition on identity documents. Those transgender-specific provisions were separate from the package's provisions on alternative marriage unions, general LGBT protections and LGBT public displays, which were framed as applying to LGBT people generally.

Legal gender recognition had been available since 2008, when transgender people could change documents and personal names after sex reassignment surgery. On 31 March 2021 the Tbilisi Civil Registry Service registered a transgender woman as female, the first such precedent. From 2024 no recognition procedure is available, so a trans visitor's passport or ID will carry whatever marker the issuing authority assigned. Legal activists had pressed for reform for more than a decade on the ground that paperwork failing to match a person's identity made job applications difficult and exposed the person to disclosure.

Transition-related care is now prohibited outright for people of all ages. The foreign agents law further endangers LGBTI service provision: organisations that refuse to register as "foreign agents" face fines and bankruptcy. ILGA-Europe reports that the anti-LGBTI law eroded trust and reduced applications for services, that large numbers of LGBTI people are leaving the country and seeking asylum documentation, and that misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

On the day after the package's final passage, transgender model and actress Kesaria Abramidze was stabbed to death; the interior ministry called it a premeditated murder. German foreign-affairs committee chair Michael Roth and EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path, and reporting after the killing described fears of hate crimes under Russia-style "gay propaganda" provisions.

Hate-crime protection exists on paper but is not enforced. Since 2012 crimes committed on the basis of gender identity are an aggravating factor under Criminal Code article 53, and Article 1 of the Law on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination, effective 7 May 2014, expressly covers gender identity and expression. There are nonetheless no official statistics on crimes on gender-identity grounds, and registered cases and studies indicate the hate-crime law is not efficient. Georgia's Public Defender reported in 2017 that prosecutors examined 86 alleged hate crimes that year, 37 of them based on gender identity; that law enforcement had no efficient strategy against hate-motivated violence and reacted only to individual cases; that numerous complaints concerned homophobic attitudes by law enforcement; and that complainants withdrew for lack of belief in a timely investigation.

Public assembly by LGBTI people has been repeatedly and violently prevented. The 17 May 2012 Identoba march was assaulted by religious counter-demonstrators, with police intervening only after fighting began and arresting victims; a 2013 rally was stormed by thousands led by priests, injuring at least 28 and trapping participants in buses and shops; the 5 July 2021 Tbilisi Pride was disrupted, leaving 53 media workers injured and NGO offices raided; and a 2021 Pride march was called off after anti-LGBT protesters stormed the Tbilisi Pride headquarters and attacked about 50 journalists. In June 2019 the Interior Ministry declared Tbilisi Pride "impossible" in its planned city-centre locations, citing safety risks, while organisers reported a week of pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel and far-right groups vowed to thwart the march. After the 2021 riots the authorities arrested 102 people, 68 of whom were released on bail and the rest held pending trial; on 9 July 2021 Tbilisi City Court denied bail and ordered pre-trial detention of four more, the judge stating the actions "in addition to being criminal, undermine the stability of the state".

A 2012 study found that 32 per cent of LGBTI respondents had experienced physical violence and 89.93 per cent psychological violence; 73 per cent of physical-violence victims never reported to police, citing ineffectiveness, fear of homophobic treatment and failure to be taken seriously, and 46.15 per cent of those who did report were dissatisfied because of homophobic police reaction.

Georgia's Constitution, adopted 13 October 2017 and in effect from 2018, provides that all persons are equal before the law and prohibits discrimination on grounds of sex or any other grounds, guarantees inviolability of human dignity with a prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, and guarantees free development of personality together with protection of life, physical integrity and liberty; universally recognised human rights apply directly and international treaties prevail over domestic acts unless they conflict with the Constitution.

Georgia does not recognise same-sex unions. The Civil Code has defined marriage as a heterosexual union since 1997, and the Constitution as passed on 26 September 2017 defines marriage solely as "a union between a woman and a man for the purpose of creating a family". A trans visitor in a relationship that would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status has no route to recognition, and the 2024 package outlaws "alternative marriage unions" outright. Same-sex sexual activity was not formally legalised until 2000, when an amended criminal code was adopted to meet Council of Europe standards; the age of consent is equal at 16 under Penal Code articles 140 and 141.
tangentialFactors:
The 2024 package drew condemnation from the European Union and human rights organisations, and the German foreign-affairs committee chair and the EU foreign policy chief described it as further derailing Georgia's EU path. The WISG and partner organisations, reporting to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers on 5 August 2024, recommended urgent action: effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, withdrawal of the proposed anti-LGBTI legislation, improved hate-crime data collection, and protection of LGBTI assembly and expression.

Reporting in October 2024 placed the measures alongside Russia-style "gay propaganda" laws and described fears of hate crimes in the conservative South Caucasus nation after the killing of a transgender actress-model.
localsOnly:
Employment discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been prohibited under Article 2(3) of the Labour Code since 2006, and the anti-discrimination law approved on 2 May 2014 and effective 7 May 2014 bans all forms of discrimination including sexual orientation, adopted as a prerequisite for EU visa liberalisation. Article 1 of that law expressly covers gender identity and expression.

LGBTI people are leaving Georgia in large numbers and seeking asylum documentation, and the anti-LGBTI law has reduced applications for LGBTI services. The foreign agents law exposes organisations that decline to register as "foreign agents" to fines and bankruptcy, endangering the provision of those services.

In July 2017 the Constitutional Court lifted the ban on gay and bisexual men donating blood as unconstitutional, following an earlier ruling of 4 February 2014, noting that modern technologies allow detection of HIV/AIDS in donations.
outOfScopeNotes:
The two source accounts give different passage dates for the 2024 package: one records passage on 4 September, another records passage by 84-0 on 17 September. The signing date of 3 October is consistent across sources. The discrepancy is unresolved.

No official statistics on crimes on gender-identity grounds exist, so the enforcement gap cannot be quantified from official data.

The most recent violence-prevalence figure in the source inventory is the 2012 survey, which predates the 2024 law and the 2021 and 2023 assembly disruptions.

Whether the 2024 package's document provisions are being applied to markers already issued is not sourced.
